question: Which statement best describes position: static (the default)?
options: relative keeps the element in normal flow and reserves its original space, but lets you nudge it visually with top/left/etc relative to where it would have been. Its most important job is creating a positioning context: it becomes the containing block for any absolutely positioned descendants, without visibly moving anything.

fixed also leaves normal flow but positions relative to the viewport, so the element stays put while the page scrolls. It's how you build sticky-to-screen headers, back-to-top buttons, cookie banners, and modal backdrops. Note: a transformed/filtered ancestor becomes the containing block instead of the viewport — a classic gotcha.

Every element is position: static by default, meaning it sits in normal document flow and ignores top/right/bottom/left and z-index entirely. You rarely write it explicitly except to reset a previously set position. Understanding static is key: the other position values are defined by how they deviate from it.

absolute removes the element from normal flow (so siblings act as if it isn't there) and positions it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor — the nearest ancestor with position other than static, falling back to the initial containing block (viewport). Offsets then place it precisely. This is the basis of overlays, badges, tooltips, and dropdowns.

question: Which statement best describes position: relative?
options: sticky is a hybrid: the element behaves like relative until it crosses a scroll threshold you set with top/bottom, then it 'sticks' like fixed within its scroll container, until its parent scrolls out of view. Perfect for sticky section headers and table headers. It only works if you specify a threshold (e.g. top: 0) and the parent has room to scroll.

Offsets (top/right/bottom/left) and percentage sizes resolve against an element's containing block. For static/relative it's the content box of the block ancestor; for absolute it's the nearest positioned ancestor; for fixed it's the viewport (unless an ancestor has transform/filter/perspective). Knowing the containing block explains where an absolute element actually lands.

z-index orders overlapping positioned elements on the z-axis: higher values paint on top. But it only works on positioned elements (not static), and it's scoped to a stacking context — created by things like a positioned element with a z-index, opacity < 1, transform, or filter. A child can never escape its parent's stacking context, which explains many 'my z-index: 9999 still hides behind something' bugs.

A reliable way to center an absolutely positioned element inside a relative parent is top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%). The offsets put the element's top-left corner at the center, and the negative-50% translate pulls it back by half its own size — working even when you don't know the element's dimensions.
